candidates.name: SIPP: historical employment-to-income transition benchmark
candidates.constructFit: Income and realised employment transitions are observable candidates; the full set of feasible income routes is not established by metadata.
candidates.longitudinal: Monthly retrospective histories support within-person timing, conditional on valid panel linkage and weights.
candidates.denominator: Civilian noninstitutionalised survey population. A baseline-employed cohort is not the total population.
candidates.timeliness: 2025 release measures 2024 and was published in July 2026. Historical-method route, not current warning feed.
candidates.access: Public-use route identified. No microdata acquired; rights, storage and output review remain pending for this project.
candidates.claimLimit: Cannot establish current income-access disruption, all feasible alternatives, causal effects or national 5% storms.
gaps: Explicit cohort, weights and variance design
Future redesign comparability and publication calendar

candidates.name: HILDA: Australian longitudinal access-pathway investigation
candidates.constructFit: Household, income, employment and health context can investigate pathways; complete access conditions are not yet mapped.
candidates.longitudinal: Annual panel with cross-wave identities and analysis-specific longitudinal weights.
candidates.denominator: Household-panel coverage and exclusions require explicit review; existing regional employment series are not linked people.
candidates.timeliness: Available Release 24 is historical. Wave 24 fieldwork spans July 2024 to March 2025; newer questionnaires are not released outcomes.
candidates.access: Research application and confidentiality deed required. Applicant eligibility, permitted environment, licence and approval are unresolved.
candidates.claimLimit: An Australian cohort cannot be joined to regional aggregates as if they describe the same individuals or prove a national storm.
gaps: Accountable eligible applicant and provider approval
Current terms and permitted processing environment
Timing alignment across income and access questions

candidates.name: Understanding Society: multi-job routes and construct-change comparator
candidates.constructFit: Multi-job detail makes this a useful comparator for alternatives, but observed jobs are not all feasible routes.
candidates.longitudinal: Annual panel; align interview dates rather than treating a wave as one calendar year.
candidates.denominator: Household survey with distinct sample components; cohort inference needs matching longitudinal weights, not an unweighted national share.
candidates.timeliness: Inspected catalogue: Waves 1-15 through 2024, April 2026 edition. Not a live warning feed.
candidates.access: Registered End User Licence route; commercial use needs owner approval. More detailed access tiers have additional restrictions.
candidates.claimLimit: Questionnaire or coding changes can resemble economic change; no current national income-access inference is admitted.

recommendation.rationale: First test a falsifiable employment-to-income transition method against documented monthly histories. This lower-access-friction benchmark does not choose the live pilot country.
conditionalOn: Release-specific metadata proves required variables and reference periods
Independent statistician accepts cohort, weights, uncertainty and identification limits
Accountable human approves project data handling and applicable rights
Analysis plan and negative-result criteria are frozen before outcome inspection
recommendation.counterargument: Accessible monthly histories can seduce us into measuring realised income instead of feasible access. Release lag and future redesign prevent a shortcut to warning skill.
recommendation.fallback: If SIPP cannot distinguish the required transition, do not substitute unemployment as access. Retain HILDA as a conditional Australian-depth route; commission only a separately approved acquisition or study proposal for missing constructs.

unresolvedDecisions.question: Does 5% mean newly affected people, an affected stock, or a percentage-point increase, and over what window?
Which loss of income-generating access is materially disruptive, and by whose standard?
How long must disruption persist, and how are interruptions or recovery treated?
How do pilot cohort, working-age population and total-country population remain distinct?
Are indirectly exposed household members counted separately from directly affected individuals?
Which alternative income routes count as feasible, adequate and acceptable rather than merely imaginable?
What evidence distinguishes voluntary or beneficial transitions from forced loss, including unequal gains?
